feature.where: Fiji Sago Palm grows in the row of unusual palms just south of our Plumeria collection, on the south side of Cypress Pond. Start from the Red Cabbage Palm at the crushed-shell path end of the row: it is a few palms in, right after the Stumpy Palm. There is no formal path through this palm collection yet. You are welcome to walk across the open grass to see the palms and read their signs. Give this one's leaf stalks a wide berth.

feature.where: From the pavilion and the raised restrooms, go to the big Manatee Rare Fruit Council sign at the north end of the Rare Fruit Garden and walk south. The jackfruit is the first tree past the sign, on your right: a dense, round-headed tree with big glossy leaves, a pale trunk and one heavy limb reaching low over the grass.

feature.where: The larger of our two Spindle Palms stands on Welcome Island, the island the driveway circles in front of the Galleria, beside a Screw Pine. It is mature enough to flower, so this is the one to check for stalks and fruit below the crownshaft. The second grows along the walkway on the south side of Big Pond, on the pond side of the path. Palms planted a few feet apart line this stretch as the walk heads toward the southeast corner and the bridge into the Rare Fruit Garden, which the Manatee Rare Fruit Council tends. Our Bottle Palms grow at the Back Gate, by the nursery entrance, and in the Butterfly Garden. The spindle shape is there year-round.

feature.where: Coming from the office, it is the first big tree you reach at the front of Cypress Pond, on the right of the crushed-shell path. To its left stand two Red Silk Cotton Trees. Their gray, spiny trunks look much like the Kapok's, but they grow in a completely different way: low, level tiers of branches, where the Kapok holds its crown high on a bare trunk. Look up to see the difference.

standard.where: Two grow at Front Pond. The easier one to see is on the west side, the side nearest the nursery, leaning out over the water; the other is across the pond, near the entrance loop of the drive. A third stands at Cypress Pond. In spring 2026 a young fern was found beside that pond as well, possibly the first new one to come up here on its own. They lean out over the pond, so the whole fountain of fronds is easier to take in from the far bank than from beside the base.
